judge_assessment.explanation: The verdict stands but the stated mechanism is refuted by the artifacts. The judge's hard failure has two conjuncts. The second — that problem 3's pairing is not declared manual — is true, and it is the right basis for rejection: worksheet.tex problem 3 says 'Show the row-by-column pairing for at least one entry', which is displayed work, and ids 8 and 10 in the same file declare exactly that kind of subresponse manual ('a dimension argument, read by hand'; 'a representation, checked by eye'), so the omission is an internal inconsistency. But the first conjunct — 'verification checks only the completed matrix' — is not what verify.json contains. Id 3 carries four separate entries of the form {"type": "eval", "expr": "a*c + b*d", "at": {"a": 2, "b": 1, "c": 4, "d": -2}, "expected": 6}, one per product entry, with each row element and each column element bound as its own named given and the note 'Row 1 of A times column 1 of B'. That expression IS the row-by-column pairing; it is the opposite of checking a completed matrix. The same holds across the file — id 1 has four entries, id 4 has six, id 8 has four plus a manual — 34 tagged checks for 10 problems, which is the highest granularity in my slice. The mathematics is entirely correct: I recomputed every sum, scalar multiple, difference, product, determinant and system in SymPy and all match. So: right verdict, wrong reason.

strengths_to_preserve: This is the reference implementation of per-slot verification in my slice. Every matrix ENTRY has its own check rather than the matrix having one — id 1 four entries, id 2 four, id 3 four, id 4 six, id 5 four, id 8 four — and the answer key's Curriculum block reports '34 tagged checks' against 10 problems. This is precisely the pattern the rest of the run needs and it should be held up as the exemplar, not merely preserved.

The pairing structure is encoded into the expression rather than flattened: `a*c + b*d` with a, b, c, d bound separately means a transposed or mis-shifted product would fail the check, whereas a single expected matrix value would not distinguish which factor pairing produced it.

Problems 8 and 10 declare their non-computational subresponses manual with precise descs — 'Written statement that AB is defined and that its size is 2 by 2 — a dimension argument, read by hand' and 'The matrix equation the student writes for the system ... a representation, checked by eye'. That is exactly the judgement the rest of the run keeps failing to make.

Problem 6 is a real application rather than a story wrapper: S is a 2x3 stock matrix, P is a 3x1 price column, the row/column labels are stated ('Row 1 of S is the north store'), the units are dollars, and the product's shape is the answer's meaning. The declared trap — adding stock counts to prices, giving 150 — is the error that shows the student never understood what multiplication is doing.

Problem 8 is the only problem where the product's existence is in question, and it asks for the dimension check FIRST ('Check that the product AB is defined, state its size, then compute it'), which is the correct order and is separately declared manual.

root_causes.description: Displayed intermediate WORK has no place in the contract even when the problem explicitly demands it. Problem 3's pairing is not an answer the machine can recompute — it is a thing the student must show on paper — so its only correct home is a `manual` entry. The author reached that judgement for two other subresponses in the same file and missed this one, and nothing in the gate chain noticed, because id 3 already had four checks and therefore satisfied every coverage rule that exists.
evidence: worksheet.tex problem 3: 'Find the product AB. Show the row-by-column pairing for at least one entry.'
verify.json id 3: four `eval` entries, no `manual` entry
verify.json id 8 and id 10: manual entries declared for a dimension argument and a representation respectively — the same class of subresponse, handled correctly
scripts/verify.py:2020 — the coverage gate only asks whether the id appears; four entries satisfy it as fully as one

root_causes.description: A single unflagged show-your-work clause carries the same REJECT weight as a sheet with dozens of unverified slots. This case scored instruction_following 1 point higher than the others in my slice (2 rather than 1) and still rejects on one clause, while its verification granularity — 34 checks for 10 problems, every matrix entry bound individually — is the best in the slice. The rubric currently gives no credit for that, so the signal the run sends back to the author system is identical for the best and the worst coverage behaviour.
evidence: official_score: instruction_following 2, total 28/32 — the highest total in my ten cases
judge_verdict manual_items_reviewed: 3, with ids 8 and 10 correctly declared
answer_key.pdf Curriculum block: 'Difficulty 1–4 of 5 across 34 tagged checks' for 10 problems
By contrast curr-376 has 11 entries for 10 multi-part problems and receives the same REJECT

improvements.title: Written explanations the worksheet demands are recorded as machine-verified rather than manual
improvements.proposed_change: Declare problem 3's shown pairing manual, matching ids 8 and 10: {"id": 3, "type": "manual", "desc": "The written row-by-column pairing for at least one entry of AB — e.g. row 1 of A paired with column 1 of B as 2(4) + 1(-2) = 6. Displayed work, read by eye."}. Enforce it generally by extending the prose scan to show-your-work verbs — 'show the', 'display', 'write out the pairing', 'circle', 'mark', 'label' — so a demand to display an intermediate requires a manual entry under that id even when the id already carries computational checks. That last clause matters: the current coverage gate is satisfied the moment an id appears, so a per-id presence test can never catch this.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem 'Find the product AB. Show the row-by-column pairing for at least one entry.' whose id carries four eval entries and no manual entry; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero naming the undeclared displayed work. Today it exits 0 — and note it must still exit 0 for the same stem WITHOUT the 'Show the...' clause, so the fixture needs both arms.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes the single gap on the strongest verification file in the slice and makes the sheet internally consistent with its own treatment of problems 8 and 10. Because the scan keys on displayed-work verbs rather than on entry counts, it catches this class on sheets that are otherwise densely verified.
improvements.risk: Medium. 'Show' appears constantly in worksheet prose as generic encouragement ('Show the work, not just the result' sits in curr-382's directions box), so the scan must be restricted to \problem segments and require an object phrase, not the bare verb. Ship warn-only for a run.

improvements.title: The rubric cannot distinguish 34 checks for 10 problems from 11
improvements.proposed_change: Add a coverage-density signal to the scoring so the instruction_following dimension separates 'thorough with one omission' from 'terminal values only'. Concretely: have scripts/score_eval_run.py compute printed-response-slots versus verify-entry count per task and surface the ratio in the report, and adjust rubric.md so a hard failure on a single undeclared subresponse in an otherwise slot-complete sheet caps the dimension at 2 rather than 1, while a sheet verifying only terminal values caps at 1. This does not rescore this run — it changes what the next run can express. I am raising it because this case is where the current rubric is least informative: curr-388 does the right thing 33 times and is scored beside sheets that never do it.
improvements.regression_test: Add a scoring-harness test with two synthetic tasks — one with an entry per printed slot and a single undeclared show-your-work clause, one with a single terminal entry per multi-part problem — and assert their instruction_following scores differ. Today the harness produces the same score for both.
improvements.expected_impact: Gives the author system a gradient to climb. Without it, the run reports that entry-per-matrix-entry verification bought nothing, which is the wrong lesson to feed back into the next generation.
improvements.risk: Medium. Slot counting is the same imperfect heuristic proposed under verify-every-printed-answer-slot, so a rubric that depends on it inherits its false positives. Report the ratio for a run before letting it move any score.

improvements.title: Integer answers print with an ASCII hyphen while the neighbouring symbolic answers use a real minus sign
improvements.proposed_change: In scripts/render_quick_answers.py, `_fmt()` returns bare `str(v)` for the int/Decimal branch and `repr(v)` for floats, so a negative number reaches LaTeX as text-mode '-3'. Every string expected, by contrast, goes through `sympy.latex(sympy.sympify(v))` and gets a proper math-mode minus. Wrap the numeric branches in math mode the same way — return '$' + str(v) + '$' (Decimal formatting is preserved because the string is built before the wrap, so a verified 6.30 still prints 6.30). Do it for int, Decimal and float alike.
improvements.regression_test: Add a case to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py rendering a verify JSON with {"id": 1, "expected": -3} and {"id": 2, "expected": "x - 7"}, and assert both rendered entries contain the same minus token (i.e. entry 1 is '$-3$', not the bare '-3'). It fails today: entry 1 renders '-3' in text mode and entry 2 renders '$x - 7$'.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes a visible inconsistency inside a single bank. In this slice alone it shows in curr-352 ('5. -1' beside '8. 7 - 24i'), curr-363, curr-369, curr-382, curr-388 and curr-400.
improvements.risk: Low. The bank is plain text by design and is never read by check_answer_key.py, so the strict per-problem answer-key binding cannot be affected. The only failure mode is a LaTeX compile error, which the existing compile-ak gate catches on the same run.

case_summary: Every number on this sheet is correct — I recomputed all five matrix arithmetic results, both inventory totals, the determinant, the 2x3 by 3x2 product and the system in SymPy, and all match the key. The verification file is the best in my slice by a wide margin: 34 tagged checks for 10 problems, every matrix entry bound individually, and the product entries encoded as `a*c + b*d` with each row and column element as its own named given so the pairing structure itself is what gets checked. Problems 8 and 10 correctly declare their dimension argument and matrix-equation representation as manual. The rejection is nonetheless correct, because problem 3 says 'Show the row-by-column pairing for at least one entry' and that displayed work has no entry — an inconsistency with the file's own treatment of ids 8 and 10. But I disagree with the judge's stated reason: verification here does not check 'only the completed matrix', it checks each entry as a pairing, which is the opposite. The real defect is narrower than the judge describes and the case deserves to be recorded as the exemplar of per-slot verification, not filed alongside the terminal-value cases.
